comments.name: Michael S. Brown, Esq.
comments.body:
1,319 characters:

---

Ellison is right about one thing: no owner can plausibly claim to have no politics. Pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. But acknowledging bias isn't the same as guaranteeing independence, and that gap is what this op-ed doesn't close.

"Straight down the middle" describes tone, not accountability. It says nothing about whether CNN or CBS runs the story that angers an administration Paramount needs something from. CBS's own settlement over the "60 Minutes" edit is exactly the precedent making viewers nervous.

Trust isn't rebuilt by declaration. It's rebuilt by structure: a real firewall between corporate interests and newsroom decisions, a standards office with teeth and public reporting, and a standing rule that no story touching the owner's business or political relationships gets softened without documented, independent sign-off. Something falsifiable, unlike "we answer to facts, not party," which every pressured owner has said.

The same test applies to Bezos at the Washington Post and Soon-Shiong at the LA Times, both of whom have made comparable assurances while quietly narrowing coverage. We'll even extend it to Murdoch and Fox, odds notwithstanding.

The ask isn't nicer language about independence. It's proof it survives the next call from Washington.

I ask (er, prompt) it a legal question and it spits out an answer and a list of references and supporting caselaw citations. As a non-techie who errs grievously on the human side, I want to say thank you for helping us understand the role of AI better.

I always return to Chomsky, Roberts and Watamull’s 2023 article in this newspaper, “The False Promise of ChatGPT”. I think it provides the basis for understanding what AI can and cannot do.

comments.name: A town
comments.body:
The failure of the enterprise in adopting AI is often a function of listening to the media and vendor sales pitches and not doing enough research and learning. If more executives, managers, and contributors invested themselves in better understanding what modern AI is and how it works, no one would fall into these expensive time-wasting traps, and entire economies would be miles ahead. Instead, articles like this one perpetuate misconceptions and the disinformation that’s stalling good AI initiatives. 

I spend most of my work time reeducating people who share the authors experience. There’s a better way and it’s possible today. It’s counterintuitive and it isn’t even that difficult, time-consuming, or expensive compared to traditional methods. The results really are like magic when used and managed properly. We use AI to solve business problems declared “impossible” for years. 

Sadly, vendors know and exploit executives’ combination of lust for achievement and slow-and-costly solution mindset to oversell marginal solutions at excessive prices using improperly applied techniques. Thus more projects continue to fail, only setting us further back in making the gains that will propel an industry or an entire country ahead.

Achievement follows when organizations shift to a focus on learning with small projects and emphasis on culture (as others have pointed out). One good win and everything else will fall into place and the narrative in articles like these will flip.

Climate change, which is now locked-in, will trigger mass movement the like we have not seen before. Just consider that half of Bengalis live less than two meters above sea level. I was lucky that I didn't have an end of the life ailment.  But I did have stage 1 lung cancer not to mention 5 spinal compression fractures from osteoporosis and I was utterly terrified.  Terrified really is the word though it doesn't begin to describe it.

What mattered most was accurate information.  Did I know what I was heading into?  Of course, not.  Did I know if I would get through this whatever it turned out to be?  Not a change.  It was a huge horrible unknown.  I will never stop being thankful for the doctors who held my hand when I was too terrified to be coherent, who who told me the truth when I was scared, who answered my questions and who coped with my horror that they couldn't necessarily predict the outcome.

I am not as sick as some of the people described.  But trust me, even a lesser version is hell.  And thankfully , 12 years later i am still here, still speaking up and still so glad I had a medical team who knew how to communicate.

This is the perfect question for a doctor with such limited communication skills. Two years later she's off cancer drugs b/c they're no longer needed. It looks like she beat it though iImmunotherapy drugs have left some lingering problems. In any case, the oncologist was wrong.

The human brain, the human thought process, the human ability to build relationships and organizations with other real people, uses a fundamentally different logic and skill that cannot be mimicked by a computer, no matter how much "compute" you give it. There are some parallels with the emergence of the internet in the early 2000s.  At first the internet was seen as some sort of "magic" that defied normal business disciplines.  It soon showed it could not defy business gravity.

In order to get value out of AI for a business, the process still requires similar discipline to deploying any technology.

1. Define clearly what the problems to solve, or opportunity to exploits, are, and what success should look like.

2. Specify how the new technology will achieve those expectations, as well as operate within the business.

3. Build / configure the new technology.

4. Test that it works as intended

5. Deploy it into the business, and monitor that it is doing what it is supposed to.

This process need not be a rigid waterfall, it can equally be exploratory and iterative, which can be very useful with a new technology where it takes time to understand it's possible uses.

Technology that operates and makes decisions based sophisticated models needs particular ongoing monitoring.  Having worked in the banking industry which already uses sophisticated models for decision making such as credit assessment, I have seen the significant level of effort needed to make sure its decision making is understood and can be regularly validated.

Businesses which pre-emptively get rid of much of their subject matter expertise "because AI will do it all now", risk very unfortunate consequences when AI runs amok.

3) US Congressperson: 25 years - 50 years.

This article rightly humanizes the trapped sailors, but it leaves readers with only half the story. The Strait of Hormuz is not merely a shipping lane; it is one of the world’s most important strategic chokepoints. Control over it creates leverage over energy, trade, insurance, and diplomacy. That broader context helps explain why civilian ships become targets during conflict—and why protecting commercial shipping is about far more than economics.

Iran bears responsibility for seizing commercial vessels and using civilian crews as leverage. Yet this crisis also raises uncomfortable questions for governments, international organizations, and shipping companies. Have they done enough to protect the people whose labor keeps global commerce moving? Humanitarian concern should include not only sympathy after the fact but also serious reflection on the incentives and policies that place civilians in harm’s way.

The moral issue runs even deeper. These sailors are not bargaining chips or statistics. They are men made in the image of God, with families waiting for them. comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
From the article: "But he also faced criticism himself, for paying a private firefighting force to set up a perimeter around Palisades Village."

I remember how many people who fled the Camp Fire which incinerated the town of Paradise, California a few years ago ended up camped out in a Walmart parking lot in Chico. 

Paradise was an inland retirement community where people moved to escape the high prices in many parts of California, so they had little resources when faced with calamity. 

A while later when wildfire tore through wealthy coastal communities those fleeing went to a Four Seasons hotel or to one of their other homes. 

The wealthy have very high carbon footprints and plenty of resources when faced with the results of those carbon footprints. The less fortunate suffer the consequences.

comments.name: BJ

While the article states that only 30% of the customers were local, it's probably going to take 5-10 years before the neighborhood is something other than a distopian moonscape. When it revives it will be different depending upon how the neighborhood redevelops around it.  Oakland Hills is the example. Altadena's resurrection will be slower and will more likely parallel that in Paradise.

comments.name: Marty in Point Loma

The scale of devastation that occurred is unreal.  That a fire and Santa Ana winds could run through an entire community with no way to stop it speaks to the force of nature - and the need to be adept at how to survive in the urban / woodland interface if you chose to live there.  

I have been watching 50 years of urban interface wildfires - now adding Spokane to the list - and it shows how incapable humans are at controlling nature.

Well deserved clearly because there is not one word about the food that is critical. Not one. That's excellent. The food seems without fault. That explains the James Beard awards, the ranking on North America's 50 Best, and the Michelin notice. The only fault found in the entire piece is the temporarily unfinished space, used for waiting now, that felt chilly and off-putting. So, is that the basis of the "Very Good" rating as opposed to, say, a rating of Excellent? I ask not because I'm arguing with the evaluation but because I'm trying to understand it and I'm trying to understand how exactly you assign it. Not just in this instance, but across the board. comments.body: Fluctuations in bilateral trade deficits may be responses to tariffs, cycles in product sales and production, seasonal factors and the like. However, the overall trade deficit is a reflection of the algebraic sum of the federal budget deficit and the margin of aggregate investment over aggregate saving. This is an accounting identity discussed in the international trade chapters of any sophomore economics text. The administration earlier this year imposed tariffs to solve a Balance of Payments "emergency" but the balance of payments deficit is always zero because the exchange rate adjusts with a floating dollar. The trade deficit is not a reflection of national honor - unless you are mostly worried about the federal deficit which is increasing under this president.

But, since we consider shareholder profits and executive compensation more of a human right here than we do actual life and quality of life of all humans, we have the system we have.

There was one phrase I heard a lot back then: baseball-style arbitration — the same system Major League Baseball uses to settle salary disputes between players and teams. Legislators planned to mimic that system to sort out cases where doctors and insurers couldn’t agree on a price for emergency services. But applying sports logic to health care hasn't worked out as planned. My colleague Margot and I set out to figure out why.
